summary.text: A 59-year-old man was referred with a diagnosis of NSTEMI after chest pain following intense physical exertion one week before admission. The pain was squeezing, with mild diaphoresis, lasted about 30 minutes and resolved spontaneously. A local hospital found a largely unremarkable ECG but markedly elevated troponin I (7.3 ng/mL); he declined the advised coronary angiography. He had well-controlled hypertension and a history of smoking.

At admission he was asymptomatic, with normal repeat ECG and high-sensitivity troponin T, a normal chest radiograph and an echocardiogram without regional wall motion abnormalities and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 65%. Coronary angiography showed no significant stenosis but a mid-LAD myocardial bridge with 100% systolic compression; IVUS showed a half-moon sign without plaque, and the resting full-cycle ratio was 0.91.

SPECT showed no significant perfusion defects at rest or with adenosine stress. MINOCA was diagnosed, likely attributable to the myocardial bridge. No interventional or surgical treatment was pursued; he was managed conservatively with aspirin 100 mg and metoprolol succinate 47.5 mg once daily, and dual antiplatelet therapy and statins were not given.

After 2 days of follow-up the ECG and cardiac biomarkers showed no significant change from baseline, he had no obvious chest tightness or pain, and he was discharged home. During 3 years of follow-up he remained free of recurrent myocardial infarction and his exertional chest pain was markedly improved.
